title: A Fish Out of Water? Ancient Predator's Brain Hints at How We Got Legs
summary:
What if the secret to how animals first walked on land was locked inside a fossilized fish skull? Researchers at Flinders University in Australia have used cutting-edge technology to peer inside the braincase of Koharalepis jarviki, a predatory fish that lived during the Devonian Period—often called the "Age of Fishes." Their findings, published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, reveal that this ancient creature had a brain surprisingly similar to those of fish that were evolving to live on land. 

The fossil, discovered in Antarctica's Lashly Mountains, is the only known specimen of its kind. It belongs to a group called the Canowindridae, which highlights the ancient connection between Australia and Antarctica when they were part of the supercontinent Gondwana. Using non-destructive neutron imaging—a technique that can reveal internal structures without damaging the fossil—the team mapped the fish's braincase and neuroanatomy. 

"We found evidence that the brain of Koharalepis was similar to those of the fishes that straddle the vertebrate water-to-land transition," said lead author Corinne Mensforth, a PhD candidate at Flinders. The scans also uncovered adaptations for life near the water's surface: openings on top of the skull for extra air intake and a pineal organ, which detects light and regulates circadian rhythms. These features suggest the fish could supplement its oxygen supply by gulping air, a crucial step for surviving in shallow, oxygen-poor waters. 

Growing to about one meter in length, Koharalepis was likely an ambush predator that relied on senses other than sight, given its relatively small eyes. It hunted smaller animals in freshwater environments. The research builds on earlier work by Flinders Emeritus Professor John Long, who first described the species in 1992. "Modern imaging technology made it possible to study internal structures without damaging the fossil," Long said. "This has enabled us to understand some of the behavior, adaptations and relationships of Koharalepis—and how fish first left the water to live on land approximately 385 million years ago." The study adds a vital piece to the puzzle of how vertebrates evolved from aquatic creatures into the diverse land animals we see today.
why_it_matters: This discovery helps explain one of the biggest transitions in the history of life: how fish evolved into land animals that eventually gave rise to humans. Understanding gradual changes in brain structure and air-breathing can also inform modern biology and medicine.

background_read: The Devonian Period (419–359 million years ago) is often called the 'Age of Fishes' because of the vast diversity of fish in oceans and freshwaters. During this time, some fish began to develop features that would later allow vertebrates to live on land. Key transitional fossils like Tiktaalik, discovered in the Canadian Arctic, show how fins could evolve into limbs.

The new study of Koharalepis jarviki, a member of the Canowindridae family, uses neutron imaging—a gentle scanning method that does not damage rare fossils—to peer inside its braincase without cutting it open. The fossil was found in the Lashly Mountains of Antarctica, but 380 million years ago this region was part of the supercontinent Gondwana, which included present-day Australia, South America, Africa, India, and Antarctica.

Flinders University (in Adelaide, South Australia) led the research, with PhD candidate Corinne Mensforth as lead author and Emeritus Professor John Long (who first described the species in 1992) as co-author. Their findings reveal that the brain of Koharalepis already had features associated with air-breathing and light detection, hinting at the gradual acquisition of traits needed for life in shallow, oxygen-poor waters—a key step before moving onto land.

perspectives.description: The study provides direct evidence of brain adaptations that helped fish survive in shallow water, a crucial step for the move to land. It also shows how advanced imaging can reveal new data from old fossils.
Relying on a single incomplete fossil can be risky; more specimens are needed to confirm that these brain features were common across the group and not just an individual variation.

The research demonstrates how non-destructive technology is transforming paleontology, allowing the re-examination of museum specimens and revealing evolutionary patterns that were previously hidden inside rock.

The findings could guide searches for additional Canowindridae fossils in Antarctica and Australia, and similar imaging may be applied to other key fossils to map the full water-to-land transition more completely.
